Shanghai Travel Guide
 Shanghai, which attracts millions of tourists every year, has consistently ranked at the top of China's most popular tourist cities. This makes a lot of people wonder — why is it so appealing? To begin with, as the most modern international metropolis in China, Shanghai boasts the largest number and tallest skyscrapers, as well as the most magnificent night views. A futuristic world constructed by scientific technology is vividly demonstrated here. While Shanghai is more than just modernization. With streets surrounded by luxuriant plane trees and numerous European-style buildings, it still retains the feeling of old Shanghai from a hundred years ago. It is precisely this blend of modernity and retro, Western and Chinese elements that gives this city its greatest charm. European-style Buildings along the Bund 
Besides, by virtue of Shanghai’s well-developed tourism supporting facilities, you will find everything here including transportation, payment, and accommodation very convenient. Moreover, as the third-largest aviation hub in the world, Shanghai has an extensive network of routes connecting to other parts of the globe, making it the first stop for countless overseas tourists when embarking on their journey to China.
AttractionsThe Huangpu River and the Bund are the must-see attractions in Shanghai. Strolling along this river, you will have a strong feeling for the contrast between the modernization and the retro charm of the city. On the east bank stand towering skyscrapers presenting a prosperous urban image, while on the west bank is the Bund with a group of century-old European-style architectures.
Yu Garden, featuring a totally different style from its surroundings, is a hidden gem in the city center. As one of the most representative classical Chinese gardens, it fully showcases the elegance of traditional Chinese architecture. Traveling farther, you will feel the diversity of Shanghai more deeply in Zhujiajiao Ancient Town. Located in the suburbs, it contrasts sharply with the hustle and bustle of the urban area. Here, you can quietly admire the bridges and flowing water and stroll along the cobblestone paths, enjoying the peacefulness of the town. If you are interested in Chinese history and culture, you will be amazed about the comprehensive collection of ancient Chinese art in the Shanghai Museum East.

TransportationShanghai is the most comprehensive transportation hub in China. It boasts extensive international and national air routes, as well as rail routes, so whether you fly directly from overseas, make a flight transfer within China, or take the high-speed train from other Chinese cities, you can smoothly reach Shanghai.
Besides, there are various transportation options for you to travel around Shanghai. Just plan your itinerary in advance and decide which mode of transportation to take. Shanghai Pudong Airport Terminal Shanghai Metro  
How to Get to Shanghai?Shanghai has two major international airports, Hongqiao and Pudong, with routes connecting to 302 destinations in 53 countries around the world. No matter where you depart from – Asia, Europe, Americas, Africa, Oceania, or from any of China’s major cities – you can get to Shanghai successfully. Additionally, the land transportation in Shanghai is well-connected. If you are going to start from any other Chinese cities, such as Beijing, Xi’an, Chongqing, Guangzhou, etc., just a high-speed rail ticket can send you directly to Shanghai.
How to Get Around in Shanghai?The public transportation system within Shanghai is both diverse and intelligent. Metro, bus, and ferry all take turns to serve your travel around the city. Among them, metro is the most recommended transportation tool, as it facilitates your journey by avoiding traffic congestion on the roads. Moreover, the subway lines cover most of the popular attractions and commercial zones in the city, which provides tourists with great convenience. However, during off-peak hours or if you want to visit some scenic spots in the suburbs, then taking a taxi is also an optimal choice. It not only enhances the travel comfort but also allows you to directly reach the destination.

Shanghai Weather & Best Time to Visit
Shanghai has a subtropical monsoon climate and characterized by four distinct seasons. January to February is the coldest period, with the temperature fluctuating between 3 to 5℃ (37 - 41℉). July to August are the hottest months, with temperatures often rising to 40℃ (104℉); and affected by oceanic climate, shanghai tends to be muggy in summer. Besides, there is rainy season in Shanghai that usually falls in mid-June to early July. Your travel experience would be compromised during this time. 
The best times to visit Shanghai are April to May and October to November. During these periods, the weather is balmy, combined with beautiful natural scenery.

Where to Stay in Shanghai?The most recommended areas to stay in Shanghai are locations near the Bund on the west bank of Huangpu River where a lot of popular attractions gather around. Also, these places feature well-connected transportation networks, providing great convenience for your trip. Furthermore, there are diverse hotels to pick, ranging from mid-range to high-end. Just standing by the hotel window, you can enjoy an enchanting night view of the Bund. However, the accommodation expenses in these areas are relatively high.
If you want to stay in a more cost-effective hotel, then locations near all the subway stations on the west bank of Huangpu River are suitable. Additionally, if you are a business traveler, then living in places on the east bank would be ideal since major conference centers are located here.
How Long to Stay in Shanghai?Tourists with a tight schedule can generally complete an itinerary in 2 - 3 days by visiting core landmarks such as the Bund, Yu Garden, Lujiazui, and Nanjing Road. If you are interested in Chinese history and culture, it’s recommended to spend an extra day to visit the Shanghai Museum East and explore the Shikumen buildings of Tianzifang. Anyway, it’s not possible to fully explore Shanghai in just one short journey since its diverse landscapes are scattered at every corner of the city. Yet regardless of how much time you spend here, you’ll always gain a precious travel memory.
Shanghai Food Shanghai Food: Pan-fried Pork Bun Shanghai local cuisine offers a balanced flavor of sweetness and saltiness. Braised pork is one of the most representative Shanghai dishes. Having been simmered slowly over a long time, the fatty part of the pork has become velvety so it melts in your mouth immediately, while the lean part has become very tender. title: 陆家嘴 - 上海金融中心摩天大楼天际线 - LoongWander
text:
陆家嘴位于上海市浦东新区黄浦江畔，是上海的金融中心与地标性文旅集聚区。陆家嘴地理范围东至浦东南路、环路，南至东昌路，西、北临黄浦江，总面积约1.7平方公里。作为上海浦东开发开放的核心地标，陆家嘴以密集的超高层建筑群、完善的金融服务体系和独特的滨江景观为核心特色，拥有多座高度位列全球前列的摩天大楼，其中上海中心大厦总高度632米，为中国第一、世界第三高楼；上海环球金融中心高度492米，金茂大厦高度420.5米，三座建筑共同构成“陆家嘴三件套”城市天际线。截至2025年，陆家嘴区域集聚了超千家金融机构、数十家跨国公司地区总部，同时融合了滨江休闲、都市观光、文化体验等多元旅游功能，年接待游客超千万人次，是上海都市旅游的核心名片。
历史文化
陆家嘴的名称源于明代翰林院学士陆深，其家族曾在此聚居，且此地位于黄浦江转弯处，形似“嘴”状，故而得名。在近代，陆家嘴曾是上海的轻工业聚集地和码头仓储区，见证了上海近代工业的起步与发展，留存有少量近代工业建筑遗迹，成为浦东历史脉络的重要佐证。
1990年，上海浦东开发开放战略正式启动，陆家嘴被确立为国家级金融贸易区，自此开启了从传统工业区向国际金融中心的转型之路。三十余年间，陆家嘴从一片农田与旧厂房区域，逐步建成集金融、贸易、旅游、文化于一体的现代化城区，其发展历程成为中国改革开放的生动缩影，也形成了“敢闯敢试、敢为人先”的浦东精神，成为陆家嘴独特的文化内核。
如今，陆家嘴在保留金融核心功能的同时，不断融入海派文化与现代都市文化，滨江大道的城市公共空间、各类艺术展馆、文化展演活动等，让陆家嘴不仅是金融高地，更是上海文化交流的重要平台，实现了经济与文化的双向赋能。
主要景点
上海中心大厦
上海中心大厦坐落于陆家嘴银城中路501号，总建筑面积57.8万平方米，建筑总高度632米，由美国Gensler建筑设计事务所设计，2016年正式投入使用。大厦共118层（地上），地下5层，集办公、酒店、观光、商业等功能于一体，其顶部的“上海之巅”观光厅位于118-119层，海拔546米，配备全球最快的超高速电梯（速度达18米/秒），仅需55秒即可从地下1层抵达观光层，游客可360度俯瞰上海全景，是陆家嘴登高观光的核心景点。
上海中心大厦
上海环球金融中心
上海环球金融中心位于陆家嘴世纪大道100号，建筑高度492米，地上101层，地下3层，总建筑面积38.16万平方米，2008年正式开业。其最具标志性的设计是顶部的“风洞”造型，94层（423米）、97层（439米）和100层（474米）设有观光设施，其中100层的悬空观光长廊采用透明玻璃地面，游客可直面脚下的城市景观，是陆家嘴极具特色的高空观光体验点，大厦同时承载国际金融办公、商业配套等功能。
上海环球金融中心
金茂大厦
金茂大厦位于陆家嘴世纪大道88号，总高度420.5米，地上88层，地下3层，总建筑面积29万平方米，1999年建成开业，是陆家嘴早期的超高层地标建筑。大厦融合了中国传统宝塔建筑风格与现代摩天楼设计，88层观光厅高度340.1米，拥有开放式的高空观景平台，可近距离观赏黄浦江两岸风光；大厦内还设有金茂君悦大酒店，占据53至87层，是世界上最高的酒店之一，成为商务与观光结合的典范。
金茂大厦
陆家嘴滨江大道
陆家嘴滨江大道西起东昌路渡口，东至浦东南路，全长约2.5公里，占地面积约10万平方米，是集休闲、观光、生态于一体的城市滨江公共空间。滨江大道紧邻黄浦江，与外滩万国建筑博览群隔江相望，沿途设置了亲水平台、观景步道、绿化景观带及各类休闲设施，游客可步行欣赏黄浦江景与陆家嘴天际线，也是拍摄上海城市景观的热门地点，每日开放时间为全天，是陆家嘴市民与游客休闲的核心区域。
陆家嘴滨江大道
上海海洋水族馆
上海海洋水族馆位于陆家嘴环路1388号，总建筑面积约20500平方米，是国家AAAA级旅游景区，2002年正式对外开放。馆内拥有长达155米的海底隧道，为世界最长的海底观光隧道之一，展示了来自全球五大洲、四大洋的超500种、超10000尾水生生物，包括中华鲟、扬子鳄等珍稀物种，是集展示、科普、教育于一体的海洋主题展馆，年接待游客超200万人次。
上海海洋水族馆
上海迪士尼旗舰店
上海迪士尼旗舰店（陆家嘴店）位于陆家嘴丰和路180号，是迪士尼在中国大陆的首家旗舰店，建筑面积约5000平方米，店内汇集了迪士尼全系列主题商品，从经典卡通形象周边到限量版纪念品，是亲子游玩与迪士尼粉丝打卡的热门地点，同时建筑外观融入迪士尼经典元素，成为陆家嘴商业文旅的特色节点。
上海迪士尼旗舰店
游玩路线
推荐陆家嘴一日经典游玩路线：上午9:00抵达陆家嘴地铁站（2号线），首先前往上海海洋水族馆（游玩约2小时），近距离观赏海洋生物；11:30前往滨江大道，沿黄浦江步行至东昌路渡口段，欣赏外滩与陆家嘴天际线，途中可在滨江休闲区稍作休息，享用简餐；下午13:30前往金茂大厦88层观光厅（游玩约1小时），体验高空观景；15:00前往上海环球金融中心，打卡100层悬空观光长廊（游玩约1.5小时）；16:30前往上海中心大厦，登顶“上海之巅”观光厅（游玩约1小时），欣赏日落时分的上海全景；18:00后可前往陆家嘴中心L+Mall或正大广场享用晚餐，餐后可在滨江大道观赏外滩夜景，结束当日行程。若时间充裕，可增加迪士尼旗舰店、陆家嘴中心绿地等点位，调整为两日游玩路线，首日侧重高空观光与滨江景观，次日侧重海洋馆与商业体验。
游玩建议
最佳游玩时间：春秋两季（3-5月、9-11月），气温适宜，能见度高，适合登高观景；若想观赏夜景，建议选择周五、周六晚间，外滩及陆家嘴灯光秀效果更佳，灯光开放时间为18:00-22:30。
登高观光建议：上海中心大厦、环球金融中心、金茂大厦任选1-2座即可，避免重复体验；建议提前1-2天在官方平台购票，可节省现场排队时间。
亲子游玩建议：优先选择上海海洋水族馆+迪士尼旗舰店的组合，海洋水族馆建议游玩时长2-3小时，避开周末及节假日高峰，每日9:00开馆时入场人流量较少。
摄影建议：拍摄陆家嘴天际线最佳点位为滨江大道东昌路渡口附近，拍摄外滩与陆家嘴同框最佳时间为日落前1小时（“黄金时刻”）；拍摄高空全景建议携带广角镜头，上海中心118层观光厅允许使用非专业摄影设备。
餐饮建议：陆家嘴区域餐饮价格偏高，可选择正大广场、陆家嘴中心L+Mall等综合商场就餐，滨江区域也有简餐咖啡店。
游玩时长：核心景点全覆盖建议1天（8小时），若包含深度体验（如酒店下午茶、展馆细逛）建议1.5-2天。
注意事项
登高观光注意：上海中心、环球金融中心、金茂大厦的观光厅均禁止携带易燃易爆物品、大件行李（超过20寸行李箱），玻璃栈道区域禁止穿高跟鞋踩踏，儿童需由成人陪同，1.2米以下儿童部分场馆免票。
人流管控：节假日（如春节、国庆）陆家嘴核心区域会实施人流管控，部分路段可能临时封闭，建议提前关注浦东新区文旅局公告，错峰出行。
交通提示：陆家嘴地铁站（2号线）节假日高峰时段会限流，建议选择14号线浦东南路站、9号线商城路站出站后步行前往，避免拥堵。
天气提示：登高观景受天气影响较大，若遇雾霾、大雨天气，能见度会大幅降低，建议出行前查询空气质量指数（AQI），AQI低于100时观景效果最佳。
财物安全：陆家嘴游客密集区域，需注意保管手机、钱包等随身物品，滨江大道等开阔区域谨防无人机、风筝等高空物品坠落风险。
设施使用：滨江大道的公共座椅、卫生间等设施免费使用，禁止占用公共空间摆摊、露营，遵守公共场所管理规定。
交通
地铁：乘坐上海地铁2号线至陆家嘴站（1号、2号、6号口出站均可直达核心区域）；14号线至浦东南路站（4号口出站，步行约800米至滨江大道）；9号线至商城路站（1号口出站，步行约1公里至陆家嘴中心区域）。
公交：陆家嘴区域公交线路有81路、82路、583路、799路、939路、961路等，陆家嘴环路丰和路站、陆家嘴地铁站站为核心公交站点，可直达各景点。
轮渡：从浦西外滩金陵东路渡口乘坐东金线轮渡至东昌路渡口，渡江约10分钟，上岸后步行5分钟即可到达滨江大道，是体验黄浦江交通的特色方式。
自驾：陆家嘴核心区域停车场主要有正大广场停车场、上海中心大厦停车场、金茂大厦停车场，节假日停车位紧张，建议优先选择公共交通。
出租车/网约车：陆家嘴区域网约车下车点主要集中在正大广场南门、上海中心大厦东门、滨江大道东昌路入口处，禁止在主干道随意停车上下客。
开放时间
全年全天开放。

title: Shanghai Jing'an Temple Travel Guide: What to See and Do
text:
Home
 Destinations
 Shanghai 
Shanghai Jing'an Temple Travel Guide: What to See and Do
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Sep. 22, 2026 
Jing'an Temple is one of Shanghai's most recognizable contrasts: a gilded Buddhist temple standing amidst a modern city with heavy traffic and beside one of the city's busiest metro stations.
If you only want Shanghai's classic temple-and-skyscraper photograph, you do not need to buy a ticket for Jing'an Temple. The exterior, nearby plaza, and surrounding streets already give you the city contrast most visitors come for.
Pay to enter only if you want to see the temple as a working Buddhist site: incense, worshippers, timber halls, and Buddhist statues at close range. That is the real choice to make before you arrive.
Is Jing'an Temple Worth Paying to Enter?
Jing'an Temple, Shanghai
Opening hours: 7:30–17:00
Entrance fees: 50 RMB/pp (free admission for seniors aged 70 and over and children under 1.3 meters in height)
Time needed: 1–2 hours
For a first visit, think of Jing'an Temple in two parts:
Exterior visit: free, flexible, and best for the iconic "golden temple in modern Shanghai" image.
Inside visit: paid admission, active worship spaces, and a closer look at the halls, statues, and ritual atmosphere.
Skip It If You Only Want a Quick Photo
The exterior is enough for a strong photograph. You can frame the golden roof with skyscrapers, moving traffic, or people crossing the plaza, creating a picture that says "Shanghai" rather than simply recording a temple facade.
Three nearby viewpoints work particularly well:
1. The pedestrian overpass at Huashan Road and Yan'an West Road gives you the widest city composition. From above, place the temple in the distance and let the traffic and towers fill the foreground. Use the railing only as a compositional line; do not climb it or obstruct pedestrians.
2. The reflecting pool near Exit 14 of Jing'an Temple Station works best when the water is still. Hold your phone low and include both the gold roof and its reflection. This is a simple, social-media-friendly shot that needs no ticket.
3. Jing'an Temple Plaza is better for a closer family or couple photograph. Step slightly away from the entrance flow, keep the guardian lions or roofline in the frame, and avoid blocking people who are arriving to worship.
Night view of Jing'an Temple, Shanghai
For daylight, the temple roof usually reads most clearly when the sky is bright.
For a darker, more cinematic image, arrive around sunset. However, to photograph the temple illuminated at night, you will need to visit between 6:00 PM and 10:00 PM on a Friday or Saturday.
If photography is your priority, a China Highlights guide can place these viewpoints into your walking route instead of sending you inside simply because the temple appears on a standard sightseeing list.
5-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou and Suzhou Explore the Elegant China
Enter If You Want to See an Active Buddhist Temple
A close-up look at the architectural details of Shanghai's Jing'an Temple.
Inside, Jing'an Temple makes sense when you want to understand it as an active Buddhist temple rather than a photogenic building.
You may see people lighting incense, praying, and moving quietly through the halls. Keep your voice low, follow signs and staff instructions, and never photograph worshippers, monks, or sacred objects without permission.
Touring the temple usually takes about one hour for the main spaces. With children, or if you want time to observe the architecture, allow longer. If your Shanghai schedule is already packed, the exterior is the better choice.
Mahavira Hall
The Mahavira Hall is the main focus of most visits. It houses a colossal silver statue of Sakyamuni Buddha—standing approximately 8.8 meters tall and weighing around 15 tons—which serves as the temple's most prized treasure.
Worshippers come here to pay their respects and pray for their families' safety and well-being, seeking to avert misfortune and clear away life's troubles and obstacles.
Jade Buddha Hall and Guanyin Hall
The side halls offer a more intimate contrast to the main hall's scale, named for a large white-jade Buddha and a Guanyin statue carved from camphor wood.
These details are best appreciated slowly. Look at the material texture, the expressions on the statues, and the relationship between the statues and the surrounding woodwork.
Worshippers typically visit the Guanyin Hall to pray for harmony in their personal relationships, while seeking physical health and the purification of karmic obstacles at the Jade Buddha Hall.
Jing'an Vajrasana Pagoda
Located in the northwest corner of the temple complex, this seven-story square pagoda is another important part of the temple's skyline.
Beyond admiring its architectural beauty, you may also join the faithful in circumambulating the pagoda three times in a clockwise direction to pray for smooth endeavors and family harmony.
Etiquette for Visitors
Please dress modestly when entering the temple;
Step over the threshold rather than stepping on it;
Light incense with your left hand; do not blow out the flame with your mouth—extinguish it by gently waving the stick instead;
Please speak in a low voice while inside the halls;
Do not block the pathways leading to the altars or incense burners;
Do not photograph Buddha statues, monks, or worshippers without permission.
9-Day Beijing ,Xian and Shanghai Tour China Family Classic Tour 
How Long Do You Need at Jing'an Temple?
30–45 minutes: exterior views and photography;
About 1 hour: a basic inside visit covering the main halls and atmosphere;
1–2 hours: a slower visit with children, photography, or more time for observation.
Jing'an Temple is close to its metro station, but the practical visit still includes reaching the entrance, dealing with tickets, and moving through a busy area.
Avoid scheduling an inside visit immediately before a timed reservation elsewhere.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
How to Fit Jing'an Temple into a Shanghai 1-Day Itinerary
Jing'an Temple, Shanghai
Jing'an Temple works well in a fast-paced route that shows several sides of Shanghai in one day: classical gardens, leafy historic streets, a modern business district, and the Bund after dark.
This itinerary is possible, but it is full. Treat the time suggestions as a framework rather than a promise.
Morning: Yu Garden and Yu Garden Bazaar (Enter as early as your ticket and opening arrangements allow, then leave time to browse the surrounding lanes and shops.)
Early afternoon: Wukang Road and Anfu Road (no need to cover every side street. The purpose of this stop is to experience the quieter version of Shanghai.)
Late afternoon: Jing'an Temple and the Shanghai CBD (Visit the exterior first. If you have checked the day's ticket information and have at least an hour available, go inside; otherwise, use the plaza and one nearby viewpoint for the temple-and-city contrast.)
Evening: The Bund at Sunset (This final stop is best kept flexible. Traffic can be slow, and sunset time changes throughout the year. )
This 1-day itinerary gives you a memorable overview of Shanghai, but it does not leave much room for long meals, shopping, or spontaneous stops. If you have 2 or more days in Shanghai, it is better to spread these areas across a slower private itinerary.

title: Shanghai Itinerary Planning Guide: How Many Days Do You Need
text:
Home
 Destinations
 Shanghai 
Shanghai Itinerary Planning Guide: How Many Days Do You Need
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Aug. 6, 2026 
Most first-time visitors wonder the same thing when planning Shanghai: if adding another day to Shanghai means taking one away from another destination, is it really worth it?
For a rather comprehensive trip, we'd like to recommend having three days in Shanghai, so you will have enough time to experience the city instead of feeling like you're checking off a list.
Instead of completing a mission of moving from one landmark to the next, we would like to take you to unfold the everyday moments that make Shanghai one of the most memorable stops on your first journey in China.
Content Preview
Why a Three-Day Stay in Shanghai
One Day in Shanghai
Two Days in Shanghai
Should You Spend More Than 3 Days in Shanghai?
Why We Strongly Recommend a Three-Day Stay in Shanghai
Most first-time visitors wonder: can't I see Shanghai's highlights in one day? Technically yes, but you may leave feeling like you only saw the cover of the book.
One or two days let you see Shanghai. Three days let you experience it.
We would like to describe Shanghai in three layers:
The historic Bund and old city streets.
The leafy, everyday life of the Former French Concession.
The futuristic energy of Pudong.
Each layer deserves its own day, so you can slow down, wander, and actually feel the contrast between them. 
Follow our three-day plan that takes you through all three layers—one day for the past, one for the present, and one for the future—at a pace that leaves room for discovery, not just checklist-ticking.
Still haven't decided when to visit Shanghai? See Best Times to Visit Shanghai to find the period that suits you the most.
Day 1: A Glimpse Into Shanghai's Past
The International Architecture Exhibition at the Bund, Shanghai
Start your morning on the Bund, walking along the historic waterfront with a guide who will bring the old buildings to life—from the grand Astor House Hotel to the iconic Peace Hotel and the former HSBC Building.
To help you create lasting memories, we offer postcards and stamps for you to choose from, so you can send a piece of the Bund home to someone special.
After lunch near Nanjing Road, continue your day to Yu Garden, a classical Chinese garden hidden in the old city. Wander through its winding corridors, koi ponds, and bizarre rockeries, while learning about the garden's remarkable story of destruction and rebirth.
If time allows, stroll along Shanghai Old Street before returning to the Bund for sunset. We suggest arriving there 30–40 minutes early to claim a good spot on the waterfront and watch the skyline transform as the city lights begin to glow.
6-Day Beijing and Shanghai Tour A Tale of Two Cities 
Day 2: Be a Part of Shanghai's Lively Present
Open-air cafes on Sinan Road in the Former French Concession of Shanghai
Your day begins beneath the plane trees of the Former French Concession. 
Start your walk at Fuxing Park, where a century ago French residents sipped coffee behind iron gates while Chinese locals could only look in from outside. Today, the park is for everyone.
Walk along Sinan Road, lined with vintage villas and quiet doorways, where your guide will share the stories of the families who once lived here. You can pause for a while at a corner café tucked inside a lilong alleyway, where modern coffee shops and bakeries now breathe new life into the old lanes.
If you are curious about Shanghai cuisine, we can arrange a cooking class at a local home—from shopping for ingredients at the market to sitting down to savor the dishes you have made.
End your walk at the Wukang Building, a ship-shaped apartment block that once housed foreign elites and now stands as a beloved landmark of modern Shanghai.
5-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou and Suzhou Explore the Elegant China
Day 3: Jump to Shanghai's Future
The Shanghai Trio at night
Today your trip will start with a ride—an autonomous one—to Shanghai Tower, the world's third-tallest building. 
Take the high-speed elevator to the 118th-floor observation deck, where the daytime panorama reveals the city buzzing with life below: cars like toys, crowds like ants.
Then your guide will lead you to step into the future at the world's first retail store operated by Gal, an embodied intelligent robot. Place your order and watch as the robot handles everything. 
If you have extra time, try ordering a takeaway delivered by drone, which typically arrives within fifteen minutes.
End your day at the DJI or Huawei flagship store, where you can test the latest drones, gadgets, and electric vehicles that are already shaping how people live in Shanghai.
Your right travel length always depends on your travel style and available time.
Of course, you can always swap part of the itinerary for attractions that match your interests, such as Shanghai Disneyland and Zhujiajiao Water Town, but you may inevitably lose some understanding of Shanghai.
Whatever you choose, this guide will help you build an itinerary around what matters most to you, not just what is popular on social media. Shanghai is not a place to rush through, but a city to immerse yourself in.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
One Day in Shanghai: See the Highlights, But Not the Whole Story
A view of the Shanghai skyline during the day
A Typical One-Day Itinerary (Ideal Timeline)
9 AM - 11 AM: Shanghai Tower
12 AM - 1 PM: Yu Garden
1 PM - 2 PM: Lunch Break
3 PM - 4 PM: The Former French Concession (With a limited day trip, you can only visit Wukang Road, and skip Sinan Park and Fuxing Park to miss a deeper understanding of Shanghai's colonial history.)
5 PM - 6 PM: The Bund (We believe the Bund is more worthwhile to spend 2 hours walking around, as you can truly step into the historical buildings and see firsthand what the Chinese have accomplished in this economic center. However, due to the limited time on a day trip, only a simple walk can be well-arranged.)
This itinerary covers four must-see sights with a well-planned schedule, and adding more is simply not feasible. As we have already considered the queues and traffic with a stress-free private transfer, you will be in good hands traveling with us.
For a self-guided day trip, taking a taxi or metro is workable, but you're very likely to encounter traffic jams or overcrowding during midday and afternoon rush hours, which may lead to a delay of subsequent sightseeing.
To enjoy a smooth one-day trip, consider starting your day at 8:00 AM to beat the crowds and avoid rush hours. Alternatively, you can also cut one attraction that you find less appealing for a more relaxed pace.
Looking for a stress-free experience? See our Shanghai Tours.
Two Days in Shanghai: Focus On the Core Sights
Explore the tree-lined Former French Concession of Shanghai
Having two days in Shanghai means you have time to feel the city from two distinct layers, but you still can't afford to squeeze all the highlights or even a side trip from Shanghai city center without sacrificing experiences or the relaxed pace.
The Bund and the Former French Concession, representing the past and lively present, are both excellent candidates for this kind of immersive experience.

Should you leave the Shanghai Pudong International Airport during a Shanghai layover? The quick answer is: yes, but only if you have 6 hours or more to spend.
Remember: your layover clock shrinks fast. Immigration, baggage, and the round-trip transfer to the city can easily eat up 2–3 hours. You need to be back at the airport at least 1.5 hours before your next flight.
Though we have listed out so many experiences, we still think a successful Shanghai layover is not about checking off as many attractions as possible. It is about choosing the right experience for the time you actually have.
So ask yourself before planning: do you have enough real city time to enjoy Shanghai, or will leaving the airport only turn your layover into a stressful race?
Things to Know During a Shanghai Layover
1. Know Your Real Available Time
2. Do You Need a Visa
3. How to Get from PVG to City Center
4. Do You Have a Payment Method Ready
5. Do You Have Internet Access
6. Where Can You Store Your Luggage
Top Things to Do During a Layover
Things to Know Before Leaving the Airport During a Shanghai Layover
If your layover is 6 hours or longer, leaving the airport is absolutely worth it.
However, if it is less than 6 hours, you are not recommended to leave the airport. Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG) has free Wi-Fi, restaurants, and duty-free shops. You will be fully entertained.
1. Know Your Real Available Time: At Least 6 Hours
Shanghai Pudong International Airport
Your layover time on your ticket is not your city time. The clock starts shrinking the moment you land.
Here is a realistic breakdown for Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG):
 Step
 Time Needed
 Immigration and arrivals (assuming luggage is checked through)
 30–45 minutes
 Transfer from airport to city center (taxi/metro/Maglev)
 1 hour
 Sightseeing at a relaxed pace
 2 hours
 Return to the airport
 1 hour
 Security and immigration for your connecting flight
 1.5–2 hours
 Total buffer needed
 Approx. 6 hours
This is why we suggest having at least 6 hours to embark on a Shanghai layover tour.
Remember always add an extra 30-minute buffer for unexpected delays, such as traffic jams, long queues, or slow immigration. It is better to arrive at the gate early than to miss your flight.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
2. Do You Need a Visa for a Shanghai Layover?
Shanghai municipality offers the Transit Without Visa (TWOV) policy for travelers, which lets you visit Shanghai visa-free for up to 10 days. See our China Visa-Free Transit Policy page.
Key Conditions
You must be traveling between two different countries/regions (e.g., USA → Shanghai → Japan).
You must have a confirmed onward ticket.
You must enter and exit through Shanghai Pudong (PVG), Shanghai Hongqiao (SHA), or certain other ports.
If you are unsure whether the policy could work for you, check with your airline or the nearest Chinese embassy before traveling.
3. How to Get from Shanghai Pudong Airport (PVG) to the City
Shanghai Maglev Train
Shanghai Pudong Airport is about 45–60 minutes from the city center. Here are your options:
Metro: Take Line 2 to People's Square or Nanjing Road to get to the Bund, or Lujiazui for Shanghai Tower. Trains run every 8 minutes from the airport between 6:00 AM and 10:30 PM. Traveling to People's Square takes about 68 minutes and costs 7 yuan.
Maglev: Experience the world's fastest train, and it takes only 7–8 minutes to travel from the airport to Longyang Road Station, where you can transfer to Metro Line 2 or 7 to the city center. Expect to pay 50 yuan for a one-way trip.
Taxi: You can find taxis outside the arrivals halls of both T1 and T2 terminals. It takes about 1 hour to get to the city center, and maybe 1½–2 hours during rush hour. Typically the cost is about 150–200 yuan for a one-way trip.
Private Transfer: We offer a secure, reliable, and fast private transfer service from Shanghai Pudong International Airport and other ports, starting at a cost of 18 USD. It is the best option for those who are looking for a hassle-free journey with efficiency and flexibility. See the details about our service.
If you have 7–10 hours, a taxi or private transfer saves you the most time. If you have 10+ hours, the metro is fine and gives you a glimpse of local life.
However, if you happen to be traveling during rush hour, choose the Maglev train back to the airport to avoid traffic congestion in case missing your next flight.
4. Do You Have a Payment Method Ready?
People in China are more accustomed to using electronic mobile payments rather than cash.
Nowadays, China is a predominantly cashless society, and international credit cards are not widely accepted outside of luxury hotels and tourist shops. You will need one of the following to pay for taxis, meals, and entrance fees:
Alipay or WeChat Pay: These are the most convenient options, and the two most widely used payment apps in China. You can link your international credit card to either app before you travel.
Cash (RMB): Still accepted everywhere, though you may receive change in coins or small bills. Exchange some currency at the airport arrivals hall—there are multiple currency exchange counters available. Avoid exchanging large amounts; a few hundred RMB is usually enough for a layover.
International credit cards: Widely accepted at major hotels, upscale restaurants, and larger stores. But hard to count on them for taxis or street food.
It's best to download and set up Alipay or WeChat Pay before you leave home. And you will need a working internet connection to activate them, which brings us to the next point.
You may need more information at: Payment Methods in China
5. Do You Have Internet Access?
Your phone will not automatically work in China due to the Great Firewall.
eSIM: Purchase an eSIM before you travel (apps offer China coverage). This gives you data immediately upon landing.
Local SIM card: Available at the airport, and remember to look for an official one, but it requires registration and can take 15–30 minutes to set up.
Roaming: Check with your home carrier. Some international plans include China coverage, but speeds may be slow.
If none of the above methods work, that's okay. You can ask airport staff for assistance in connecting to the airport's free Wi-Fi to complete all the setup and registration.
And it's best to download offline maps of Shanghai (Google Maps is not very stable in China, so Baidu Maps or Gaode Maps are recommended), and save your hotel or attraction addresses in Chinese characters to show taxi drivers.
See our How to Use Your Cell Phone While Traveling in China.
6. Where Can You Store Your Luggage?
If you are carrying luggage, you won't want to drag it around the city.
There are five luggage deposit offices in Terminal 1 and Terminal 2 at Shanghai Pudong International Airport.
Terminal 1: Near Gate 4–5 and Gate 10–11 in Departures Hall, and near Gate 6–7 in Arrivals Hall. Tel: 021-6834 6324.
Terminal 2: Near Service Counter A and Service Counter M in Departures Hall, and near the International Arrivals exit. Tel: 021-6834 0076.
This may cost you approximately 50 RMB per day for large items, while smaller luggage is cheaper.
Our advice: Store your luggage in the same terminal you will depart from, so you can pick it up on your way to check-in without backtracking.

title: Shanghai Weather in April 2027: Cool, Drizzles, and Blossoms
text:
Home

Shanghai Weather in April 2027: Cool, Drizzles, and Blossoms
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Jun. 5, 2026 
April is one of the most comfortable times to visit Shanghai as a spring month. 
As a first-time visitor, if you're worried that spring rain or changing temperatures could ruin the trip you've been planning, April is usually much easier to travel than you expect.
The temperatures are usually mild between 11–19°C (52–66°F), the city starts turning green again, and long walks become enjoyable instead of exhausting. 
At the same time, spring weather here can shift quickly: one day might feel bright and warm, while the next turns gray, breezy, and lightly rainy. 
Shanghai in April is often at its best when you stop treating the city like a checklist of sunny-day photo spots and start planning with a little flexibility instead.
Shanghai in April Is More About Walking Comfort Than Perfect Blue Skies
Taking a walk along Sinan Road in Shanghai in April is a very pleasant experience.
Why visit April? Because walking is one of the most immersive ways to explore Shanghai, and April offers comfortable daytime temperatures averaging 15–19°C (59–66°F), while nights drop to 10–13°C (50–55°F). 
However, temperatures can dip 2–3°C (4–5°F) after a rain shower, and the city's riverside location means evenings near the Bund or on a Huangpu River cruise can feel cooler due to wind.
You may also worry about the rain, and it's true that April brings unpredictable drizzles, with 10–12 rainy days throughout the month on average. But most are light showers lasting less than an hour, posing no threat to your well-planned itinerary.
April may not offer clear skyline views with guaranteed sunshine and a postcard-perfect blue background. On the bright side, you can enjoy mild days to explore on foot for hours without sweating or shivering, and gain a much deeper feel for the city with a leisurely pace.
Flexible Itineraries Work Better Than Fixed Plans in April
April weather in Shanghai is changeable, and light rain can appear on cloudy days without warning. Instead of fighting the forecast, adjust your daily rhythm to match the conditions.
Start earlier than you would in summer. In April, mornings are often clearer and less crowded, and this is your quiet window. For example, before 9:00 am, the Bund is often quiet enough for unobstructed skyline photos. By 10:00 am, big tour groups start arriving.
Don't put all your night views on the same day. Evening visibility varies. If one night is hazy or rainy, save your Bund walk or Huangpu River cruise for another evening when the sky is clearer.
Keep one flexible afternoon for weather swaps. Leave at least one afternoon in your itinerary with no fixed bookings. If a sunny day appears, use it for skyline views; if it rains, move indoor activities to that slot.
Expect to walk more than you originally planned. You'll find yourself strolling between neighborhoods rather than taking taxis, and April's mild weather makes walking a joy.
Save Skyline Views and Riverfront Nights for the Clearest Day
The Bund is a must for all first-timers to Shanghai.
It is a must for most first-timers to Shanghai to witness its famous skyline, where the Bund's historical buildings face Pudong's futuristic towers. You can have its best look on a clear, dry day. 
On overcast or rainy days, the tops of skyscrapers can disappear into the clouds, so you can see nothing even on the high-altitude observation decks, and night photos turn out flat and blurry.
Check the forecast each morning. When you see "sunny" or "partly cloudy," prioritize these experiences: 
Ascend Shanghai Tower or Oriental Pearl Tower in the late afternoon for golden hour light, then stay for the city lights.
Walk the Bund around sunset or sunrise.
Book your Huangpu River night cruise for that same evening.
If you're planning only two or three days in Shanghai, deciding which experiences to keep flexible can make a surprisingly big difference. We (China Highlights) often help travelers build itineraries that include weather backup options. 
However, we also recommend staying near the Bund, so even if the weather isn't good when we take you there during the day, you can still try your luck and see a clear night view every evening.
Cloudy Days Are Better for Walking and Neighborhood Exploring
You can also explore the neighborhood by bicycle on a dry day.
Cloudy skies in April are common, but they don't ruin your trip. In fact, diffused light is perfect for long walks.
The French Concession feels cozy under overcast skies: plane trees are sprouting new green along the streets, and the lack of harsh shadows makes the Art Deco villas and café terraces look soft and inviting.
For a cherry blossom hunt, Gucun Park's late-blooming varieties are equally charming without glaring sun. You can stroll the 1km-long cherry blossom avenue leisurely, feeling the gentle spring breeze caress the petals and your cheeks.
Explore Yu Garden, and you can linger by the koi ponds and zigzag bridges without constantly looking for shade.
Embrace the gray days, and you will be rewarded with Shanghai's moody, cinematic aspect.
18-Day Epic China Tour Including Yunnan and Tibet See the Incredible Beauty of Southwest China 
Light Rain Is Not Necessarily for the Worse
A boat trip in Zhujiajiao Water Town in early April is quite pleasant.
A sudden spring shower in April rarely lingers for more than 40 minutes.
Don't run back to your hotel. Instead, duck into a nearby café or hop to an indoor attraction like a museum or a gallery. What's more, light rain can actually enhance certain experiences. 
Zhujiajiao Water Town and Tongli Water Town on a drizzly day look exactly like a traditional Chinese ink painting, where you can admire mist over canals, wet stone bridges, and gray eaves against white walls.
The Jade Buddha Temple feels more serene with rain pattering on the roofs, and you may encounter lazy orange cats in the temple, leisurely taking a nap on the stone bricks.
Some of the best photos may be taken in the rain or right after the rain stops, when unexpected surprises often occur.
Is April Better Than March or May for Visiting Shanghai?
April strikes a near-perfect balance, feels more relaxed than summer and more alive than early spring, which is ideal for most travelers to explore Shanghai on foot.
Compared to March, which can still feel like winter with cold, damp days and bare trees, April brings warmer days and spring greenery, with colorful, fully blooming flowers.
Compared to May, which often sees rising humidity and sticky, uncomfortable days, April's air is still fresh and light. You can also expect heavier rains and the build-up to summer crowds.

What to Pack and Wear in Shanghai in April
Shanghai can get colder on rainy days in April, so you'll need to wear extra layers.
April's weather is generally mild, but early April can still be cool, and late April can feel like early summer.
Early April (1st–10th, including Qingming Festival)
Early April could still be cool. No need for heavy winter gear, just pack long-sleeved shirts, a light sweater, and a waterproof jacket for drizzles. A coat is fine for early mornings and evenings.
Comfortable walking shoes and a foldable umbrella are essential for strolling around, and you can bring your sunglasses for sunny afternoons.

title: Shanghai Weather in August 2026: Hot, Typhoon, Travel Tips
text:
Home
 Destinations

Shanghai Weather in August 2026: Hot, Typhoon, Travel Tips
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Apr. 16, 2026 
August is one of the hottest months to visit Shanghai, coinciding with the summer vacation. 
The weather is similar to July, with average temperatures ranging from 26–31°C (79–88°F), cooling slightly toward the end of the month. Data from August 2025 shows daily averages of 31°C or higher, with a peak of 39°C (102°F) on August 24th.
The plum rain season, with consistent rainy days, ends in July.
In August, rainfall is largely driven by typhoons, and becomes more frequent as the month progresses, averaging 10 rainy days (about 112 mm / 4.4 inches). This brings extreme weather swings, from heavy downpours to clear skies.
Is August a Good Time to Go to Shanghai?
Our clients are having a great time in the Yu Garden in August, Shanghai
Generally, we recommend avoiding July and August. September to November or March to May are much more comfortable and less crowded. 
But if August is your only option, don't worry. With a bit of planning and the right strategies, you can still have a great trip.
1. Protect Yourself From the Heat
Shanghai's August temperatures are high, often above 28°C (82°F) by 8 AM. 
For outdoor activities, bring a small handheld fan, cooling wipes, a sun hat, and a sun umbrella. If you travel with us (China Highlights), our guides will adjust your pace and provide plenty of bottled water to keep you hydrated and safe from heatstroke.
2. Plan Indoor Activities You'll Enjoy
To beat the heat, you should stick to air-conditioned indoor spots and wait for the cool moment after sunset. 
Pick what suits you the most, lose yourself in the art galleries and history museums, or shop near your hotel. You could also simply nap at your hotel or take a dip in the pool.
10-Day Leisure River Cruise Getaway TourBeijing - Chongqing - Yangtze River Cruise - Shanghai 
3. Book Early to Lock In Better Prices
August is a peak travel season, and the Chinese summer vacation. 
You can expect bigger crowds, higher prices, and limited tickets. We suggest booking your trip at least three months in advance for better rates and a smoother experience. 
What's more, planning your trip on weekdays rather than weekends, especially Tuesdays and Wednesdays, is much quieter and more enjoyable.
4. Will I Be Affected by the Typhoon?
Shanghai's typhoon season is mainly from July to September, with peak periods in late July and late August. 
But it usually doesn't pose a significant threat, since typhoons may affect flights only for 1–3 days. Check the forecast before you go, keep your bookings flexible, and leave some buffer time in your itinerary in case of delays.
8-Day Beijing–Xi'an–Shanghai Tour China Golden Triangle
What to See and Do in Shanghai in August
Spots with Air-conditioning
Enjoy the light show at the Shanghai Museum (East Branch)
Nearly every indoor space in Shanghai has air‑conditioning—from small street shops to large malls and attractions. 
We recommend choosing one larger indoor venue where you can easily spend half a day without wasting time moving between places.
Shanghai Museum (East Campus): One of China's top four museums, housing half of Shanghai's cultural relics. Explore over 20 zones featuring bronzes, sculptures, jade, ceramics, and more. There's also a dining area, which is perfect for spending a fulfilling half-day immersed in history and art. (Closed on Tuesdays)
Oriental Pearl Tower: A landmark of Shanghai. Compared to other skyscrapers, it offers a one-stop experience with observation decks, dining, and entertainment. This could be the first choice for multi-generational families traveling with kids or seniors.
Shanghai Astronomy Museum: The world's largest astronomy museum. With the theme "Connecting People and the Universe," its rich exhibits make you feel like you're turning through the pages of cosmic history. Your day here will be both educational and funny, making adults and kids fascinated by space, which will linger. (Closed on Mondays)
Xintiandi: If you're not keen on history or art, come here to enjoy the AC, shop, and stroll. This area uniquely blends traditional Shikumen architecture with modern commerce. You can truly feel "modern China" while finding great restaurants and trendy brands to shop and relax.
Outdoor Spots to Escape the Heat
Take a boat tour in Zhujiajiao Water Town, Shanghai
August in Shanghai is hot, but skipping these iconic places might feel like missing out. Choose based on your interest, and our guides will adjust the pace and commentary to give you the best possible experience.
Yu Garden: If you're not planning to visit Suzhou, this is your best window into classical Chinese garden aesthetics. Built 500 years ago, it has been restored multiple times yet still retains its charm. With plenty of shaded paths and water features, it offers slight relief from the summer heat.
Zhujiajiao Water Town: Known as "Shanghai's Venice." You can stroll along the ancient streets and experience the authentic daily life of the locals. Located by the water, it's cooler than the city center, and you can also choose to take a boat tour to relax.
French Concession Citywalk: This is a must when you want to see the blend of Western and Chinese architecture and witness the traces of Shanghai's colonial past. The plane trees along the streets provide some shade from the harsh sun. Why not grab an iced Americano at a trendy café to add a refreshing touch to your walk?
Vibrant Nighttime Activities
Take a night cruise on the Huangpu River to view the Bund, Shanghai
August evenings in Shanghai are vibrant and full of energy. The heat fades, and the city lights up.
To explore Shanghai's vibrant nightlife, you can enjoy the night view from the citywalk, embark on a food adventure at the night market, or go to the bar street for drinks and dancing.
The Bund: Stroll along the waterfront promenade and take in the iconic contrast: historic colonial buildings on one side, futuristic skyscrapers like the Oriental Pearl Tower and Shanghai Tower on the other. The cool river breeze and dazzling lights make it a perfect evening escape.
Night Cruise on the Huangpu River: To avoid the crowds, you can hop on a sightseeing boat for a 45–60 minute cruise. You'll get a panoramic view of both Puxi and Pudong skylines, with all the landmarks illuminated. It's a relaxing and romantic way to see Shanghai at night.
Huaihai Road Bars: When it comes to bar streets with a strong social atmosphere, Huaihai Road bar street is a must-mention. It is lined with stylish bars, from rooftop lounges to hidden speakeasies. You can grab a drink, unwind, and soak in the cosmopolitan night vibe in the dancing pool. This is perfect for ending a hot summer day on a cool note.
What to Pack and Wear in Shanghai in August
August in Shanghai is hot, humid, and prone to sudden typhoon-driven downpours. 
You should pack lightweight, breathable clothing, such as short-sleeved T-shirts, shorts, or wide-leg pants, and a sun-protective jacket. Opt for comfortable sneakers and sandals, and choose light-colored, quick-drying fabrics.
A portable raincoat or poncho is essential, since typhoon winds can break a regular umbrella. Still, carry a dual-purpose umbrella for light rain and sun. Don't forget high-SPF sunscreen and sunglasses.

text:
Home
 Destinations

Shanghai Weather in December 2026: Cold, Dry, and Festive
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated May. 8, 2026 
December marks the start of Shanghai's off-season. The weather turns colder, with average temperatures ranging from 4－11°C (39－52°F). January is actually the coldest month, so December is chilly but not extreme.
December is also the driest month of the year, typically seeing only 4－5 days with 33mm (1.3 inches) of precipitation. Rain is most common in early to mid-December, often coinciding with the first real temperature drops. 
During the coldest spells, light snow is possible, though in the past three years (2023－2025), winters have been relatively warm and snowfall rare. For example, in December 2025, daytime temperatures averaged around 17°C (63°F).
Even so, cold fronts can still arrive suddenly. We recommend preparing layers of warm clothing to cope with sudden temperature drops, even if most days feel mild.
Is December a Good Time to Visit Shanghai?
Yes, as the off-season in Shanghai, traveling in December means you can enjoy fewer tourists, lower prices, and uncrowded attractions. Not to mention the clear days with not-that-cold weather.
However, note the holiday period from December 20 to January 1, when Christmas and New Year's Eve celebrations bring in larger crowds, especially at popular shopping areas, Disneyland, and the Bund. 
You can easily avoid these dates for swarming crowds and temporary price increase. But if you enjoy festive atmospheres, this is actually a wonderful time to experience a unique Western-style Christmas with a Shanghai twist.
8-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou Family TourShanghai-Hangzhou-Wuzhen-Suzhou 
What to See and Do in Shanghai in December
As one of China's most international cities, Shanghai starts building its Christmas atmosphere as early as November, when the lights, trees, and window displays start to create a joyful mood.
By December, the city is at its most festive, with strong Western holiday vibes you might find surprisingly familiar yet refreshingly different.
Enjoy Christmas and Holiday Festivities
Shanghai Disneyland's Winter Frozen Parade
By early December, shopping malls and public squares are decorated with towering Christmas trees, twinkling lights, and elaborately arranged shop windows. 
To capture the most festive moments, you can spend some good time at Shanghai's famous German Christkindlmarkt on the Bund. 
Among several Christmas markets around the city, this one offers authentic German, Austrian, and Serbian cuisine. After 5 PM, a giant Christmas tree will be lit up, accompanied by live music and artificial snowfall, creating a truly festive Christmas atmosphere.
For an unforgettable experience with your family, you can spend a day at Shanghai Disneyland, which transforms into a winter wonderland with a "Snowy" castle, special parades, and holiday-themed fireworks.
Just remember to book Disney tickets at least two weeks in advance, as dates close to Christmas sell out.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
Participate in New Year's Eve Celebration
Enjoy the night view of the Bund in Shanghai
The night of December 31 is lively across Shanghai. The most iconic (and crowded) spot is the Bund, where thousands gather to watch the countdown and a spectacular light show across the skyline. 
For a less crowded experience, book a ticketed event at the Shanghai Tower or Oriental Pearl Tower. They both offer observation deck parties with champagne and panoramic night views. 
Another option is taking a Huangpu River cruise with dinner and a live DJ, followed by a countdown party and a light show on the water. 
Whichever you choose, arrive early, dress very warmly (evening temperatures can drop near freezing), and well-plan your transportation back. 
Special Note
Although subway lines usually extend their operating hours on New Year's Eve, they generally close around 1 a.m. at the latest, so you might miss or be unable to attend the countdown party. Additionally, due to the large crowds, taxis may be difficult to hail.
Embark on Warming Food Adventures
Try Shanghai Shengjian bao (pan-fried buns)
December's cold weather is the perfect excuse to enjoy Shanghai's best warming foods. 
For a local specialty, hunt down Shanghai century-old stores for xiaolongbao (soup dumplings) at the classic spot called Nanxiang Steamed Bun Restaurant (南翔馒头店) near Yu Garden, or shengjian bao (pan-fried pork buns) at Da Hu Chun (大壶春) located at Middle Sichuan Road. 
On a chilly afternoon, step into a traditional tea house for a pot of West Lake Longjing tea, or try a modern café for a heart-warming coffee at Starbucks Reserve Shanghai Roastery.
What to Pack and Wear in Shanghai in December
December in Shanghai is cold and dry. However, the past few years have seen occasional warm spells, with daytime highs reaching around 17°C (63°F), so remember to keep yourself layered to stay comfortable.
Start with a long-sleeved thermal base or a cotton shirt, add a sweater or fleece, and top with a jacket or wool coat. If you plan to be outdoors on New Year's Eve, when temperatures can drop near freezing, a heavier coat and scarf will be welcome.
Shanghai is best explored on foot, and cold winds can make comfortable walking boots essential. Rain is rare in December, but a small folding umbrella or a packable windbreaker is still useful.

Top 10 Shanghai Facts You Should Know
Chinese Name: 上海 (shàng hǎi)
Administration Type: Municipality
Area: 6,340 sq km (2,458 sq mi)
Resident Population: 24.8745 million (by 2023)
Area Code & Zip Code:
Area Code: 021
Postal Code: 200000 - 202100
Location: Yangtze River Delta, East China (31° 14' N, 121° 29' E)
1. China’s Largest City
Shanghai is certainly not the largest city in China for its geographical area, but it ranks China’s largest city in terms of the population. Although its total area is 6,340 square kilometers (2,458 square miles), ranking the 33st in China, there are over 24 million people living there, leading to a population density of 3,920 per square kilometer. 
2. One of the World Financial Center
Over the past two decades, Shanghai has thrived. In the top ten global financial centers list released by the Global Financial Centers Index in 2024, it ranks sixth and third in Asia. Many businesses have flourished in Shanghai, providing new opportunities for China's growing middle class and foreigners who want to enter the Chinese market.
3. A Multi-cultural Metropolis of History and Modernity
In terms of cultural and historical facts about Shanghai, the colonial past makes it unique from other cities in China.  
 a. Originally, it was a small fishing and textiles town who did not gain its identity until it was opened to foreign powers in the 1842 Treaty of Nanking. The British, French, Americans, Germans, and Russians started to move in. 
 b. The city flourished as a cosmopolitan and thriving commercial and financial center, dubbed the Paris of the East in the 1920s and 1930s. Many westerners set distinct western-style banks, trading houses, and mansions, leaving a totally different architectural legacy. Although erected during different periods in varying styles, such as Gothic, Romanesque, or Baroque, those buildings exist harmoniously. Many of the buildings we see on the Bund and in the Former French Concession were built during this period.
 c. In 1990, it was chosen to spearhead modern China’s reform and opening up, which resulted in intense development. 
 d. At present, it is probably the most evocative city for an outsider to visit all of the country. Its modern and ever-expanding skylines include the emblematic Oriental Pearl Tower, the soaring modern art-deco Shanghai Tower and the 101-floor World Financial Centre .
 Oriental Pearl Tower and Shanghai Tower  
4. 30-day Visa-free and 240-Hour Visa-Free Transit is implemented in Shanghai
China has implemented a 30-day visa-free policy for citizens of 38 countries including France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Malaysia, Switzerland, Australia and Japan. Starting from November 30, 2024, citizens of these countries can enter China without a visa, and the maximum length of stay is 30 days. Currently, the number of countries whose citizens can enter China without a visa has increased to 65.
Also, 240-hour Visa-free transit is implemented in Shanghai for foreign citizens from 54 countries, including Canada, Brazil, Denmark, France, UK, USA, Italy, Japan, Poland, etc.
More to see: 
China Visa-free Policy
240-hour Visa-free Transit in Shanghai
15-day Visa-Free Policy for Cruise Tour Groups to Shanghai 
5. Shanghai's transportation system is one of the best in China
As one of the transportation hubs in China, visitors can directly reach Shanghai from numerous important cities from abroad by air. The city has two international airports, respectively Pudong International Airport and Hongqiao International Airport. Its four railway stations take visitors easily to their destinations in China through trains, including the high-speed trains. Moreover, the top priority to travel around in downtown is metro for its high speed, safety, and convenience. There are 20 subway lines and 1,596 bus lines operated, passing by a vast majority of famous scenic spots, like People’s Park, The Bund, Xintiandi, Oriental Pearl Tower, Yu Garden, Confucius Temple…  
 Shanghai Subway  
6. Spring and Autumn are the Best Time to Visit 
The best time to visit Shanghai is in its spring and autumn, when the climate is neither too hot nor too cold. Belonging to the subtropical maritime monsoon, spring here usually from March to May and autumn from October to middle November, are always warm and pleasant, making it comfortable to go outside. 
7. A Sleepless City 
The colorful nightlife makes it a sleepless city, which is one of Shanghai interesting facts that you should know. When night comes, all lights shine brightly from every direction. At this time, a Huangpu River Cruise will take visitors to appreciate the charm of night scenes on both sides. In addition, most people prefer to spend free time after dark along Nanjing Road Pedestrian Street, where they may have a big bargain for small products, or enjoy some snacks and street food. Despite these, Xintiandi is a favorable place for its distinctive buildings, most of which are used as themed restaurants, art galleries, fashion shops, café shops or bars. Moreover, Hengshan Road cultivating bars in great number can be one of the most bustling places there at night.   
 Nanjing Road  
8. A Shopping Paradise
Hailed as the Shopping Paradise, Shanghai offers consumers a variety of products to choose, from high-end international brands to cheap local products. The famous shopping areas include Nanjing Road, Huaihai Road, North Sichuan Road, Xintiandi, Yuyuan Bazaar, Xujiahui Shopping City, New Shopping City and Tianzifang, from either of which, visitors can always get a satisfactory good. In addition, shopping malls are worth a visit, like Department Store and World Daimaru Department Store.  
9. Shanghai is surrounded by ancient water towns.
Outside the bustling downtown area, there are many famous water towns lying around the city, including Zhujiajiao, Zhouzhuang, Tongli, Wuzhen, Xitang, Nanxun , Qibao, and Luzhi. They are characterized by burbling brooks, arched bridges, slab-stone paved alleys, waterside teahouses and white-washed traditional style dwellings. Wandering through these waterside ancient towns to experience the locals’ leisure life style as well as appreciating the living cultural heritage will be one of the highlights of your trip. 
 Qibao water town  
10. Shanghainese tend to have a Sweet-tooth. 
Shanghai cuisine is renowned for its unique flavor profile, with a prominent characteristic being its delightful sweetness. Sugar is a core ingredient, skillfully used to create a variety of mouthwatering dishes. For example, the well-known Pineapple Sweet and Sour Pork features a perfect balance of tangy and sweet flavors, and the steamed buns with sweet meat filling are also a local favorite.

Shanghai Weather
Located in subtropical monsoon climate zone, Shanghai is relatively humid, and has four distinct seasons: pleasant and warm spring from March to May, stuffy and humid summer lasting long from June to September, comfortable and cool autumn from October to November, and overcast and a bit cold winter from December to February.  Shanghai Night View  
Temperature
There are big temperature differences between seasons: the temperature can reach above 35°C (95°F) in summer, drops to around 0°C (32°F) in winter, and stays around 10-25°C (50-77°F) in spring and autumn. Therefore, it is necessary to further check the detailed temperature situation of your planned travel dates. 
High/Low Temperatures of Shanghai
The Hottest Months of Shanghai
The hottest months of Shanghai are July and August with the daily high temperature generally above 30°C (86°F) and around 35°C (95°F), and the apparent temperature on some days is high at a level that may make you feel uncomfortable. Specifically, there are usually around 10 days when the high temperature is no less than 35°C (95°F) per month. It is not surprising at all if the daily maximum temperature exceeds 40°C (104°F) or above during this period. For example, in July and August 2024, Shanghai experienced three days when the daily high reached 40°C (104°F). 
The Coldest Month of Shanghai
The coldest month is January, but it is not severely cold here, when the daily high can reach 10 - 15°C (50-59°F) and the daily low is around 0 - 5°C (32-41°F). Even on the coldest day in this period, the temperature usually stays from -5°C (23°F) to 0°C (32°F). In some years, Shanghai may not see temperature below 0°C (23°F) at all.
Precipitation
The city receives high precipitation of around 1,200 mm annually, and it mainly concentrates in: (1) the plum rainy season from mid-June to early July, when Shanghai sees consistent rain, high humidity, and relatively short sunshine hours; and (2) the typhoon season from late July to September, when strong wind and heavy rain may hit Shanghai. The monthly average rainfall during these months ranges from 135 mm to 159 mm, and the number of rainy days per month exceeds 10. In the rainiest month of Shanghai, June, the rainy days are about 15. In other words, visiting Shanghai from June to September, there is a quite high possibility of being caught by rain.
Average Precipitation of Shanghai
Does it Snow in Shanghai?
In Shanghai, the probability of snow is low. The annual average snowy days are only about 1 to 5, concentrated from late December to the next February, with some years experiencing no snow at all. On these possible snowy days, light snow and sleet are more common. Besides, it’s hard for you to see snow cover in Shanghai due to the not low enough temperature.
Humidity
The air is relatively wet in Shanghai nearly all year round. On average, the humidity is no less than 70% every month. During the quite rainy period from June to September, the average humidity is around 75%. Such humidity levels produce some effect on apparent temperature: in summer, it makes you feel hotter and more stifling; in winter, it makes you feel clammy.
Humidity of Shanghai
Best Time to Visit Shanghai
Springtime, from March to May, and autumn, from October to November, are regarded as the best times to pay a visit to Shanghai. Traveling to Shanghai during these two periods, you will feel neither cold nor hot. Besides, you seldom encounter quite rainy weather in these months. As for the scenery, with colorful flowers or autumn leaves, it will not let you down.
If possible, when planning a Shanghai trip in 2026, avoid July to August with large travel crowds, scorching hot weather, and frequent summer showers.

Shanghai Climate - Seasons & Travel Recommendations
Spring: March - May
Weather: Spring in Shanghai is from March to May. This is one of the best seasons of the year for traveling. The temperature is at a comfortable level. Light rain happens, however, does not disturb your trip much. Spring flowers in bloom make the city lively and attractive.
Clothes: Most of the time, short-sleeved or long-sleeved shirts plus thin jackets and jeans are suitable outfits. However, in early March, relatively thick coats is necessary.
Travel Recommendations: With cozy temperature and mostly sunny climate of Shanghai, spring is a perfect time to both admire the cultural attractions like The Bund & Huangpu River and Jade Buddha Temple and explore the natural beauty like in Zhujiajiao Water Town. Pay attention to the occasional large temperature difference between day and night.
 See also: 15 Most Beautiful Places in Shanghai in Spring Lush Yu Garden in Spring 
Summer: June - September
Weather: Summer here is long from June to September. With high temperature and a lot of rainfall that accounts for over 50% of the city's annual total, Shanghai at this time can be uncomfortably hot and humid, especially in July and August, when the temperature reaches 35°C (95°F) or above quite often. 
Clothes: Wear clothes like breathable and lightweight tank tops, T-shirts, skirts, and shorts to keep cool in summer with high temperature and humidity. Besides, an umbrella is a must in rainy summer. Hot Summer with Intense Sunshine 
Travel Recommendations: Considering the heat, you are recommended to visit outdoor attractions in the early morning, late afternoon, and at night, the relatively cooler periods. As for the hottest period from about 12:00 to 14:00, you’d better visit indoor attractions like Shanghai Museum or just stay at hotels or restaurants to rest. 
 See also: 12 Popular Shanghai Activities to Survive Summer
Autumn: October - November
Weather: The short autumn comes in October and November. In this season, the weather turns cool and pleasant. The flood season has ended, and you will not experience much rain. In conclusion, the temperate weather makes this season a good travel time. 
Clothes: Long-sleeved shirts plus thin jackets are appropriate. Bringing a thicker coat when visiting Shanghai in late November is a clever decision. People Playing Taichi in Cool Autumn 
Travel Recommendations: With such wonderful weather conditions, you can enjoy a city tour comfortably, like taking a Huangpu River cruise to see western buildings of the Bund and modern skyscrapers in Lujiazui, visiting the busy Nanjing Road, and admiring the Yu Garden. If you travel to Shanghai in late autumn, you can see it decorated by the golden autumn leaves. 
 See also: Where to Go in Shanghai in Autumn - 11 Best Destinations
Winter: December - February
Weather: The city's temperature in winter is not as low as in northern China like Beijing, and the worst of the cold usually lasts for just a few days in late January, the only period when the daily low may drop below 0°C (32°F). However, humid cold wind may blow sometimes, making the apparent temperature much lower. Winter is the period with the lowest rainfall all year round, when Shanghai only sees a little rain or snow. Shanghai Nightlife
 Night View of Huangpu River 
 and the Bund 
Night life in Shanghai is gentle and colorful because life here is much more than life itself. It is elegant.
The scenery at night has to be seen and the Bund is a must. The ornate classical and modern buildings take on a new and exciting look as they are lit up by an abundance of colored lights. Looking across the Huangpu River to the Oriental Pearl TV Tower and Jinmao Tower is a magical sight. A night-time Huangpu River cruise presents a wonderful opportunity to appreciate the night life on the Bund. 30 or so boats carry tourists. These include deluxe boats, ancient dragon boats of Ming and Qing styles, boats of Shikumen style of old Shanghai, Pirate Boat, etc. The boat fare is CNY 120 for a classic ride and CNY 128 to 188 for a luxury ride. Whatever kind of boat you take, the view to be seen here at night will be sure to live on in your memory for years to come.
Leaving the scenery aside, walking westward along Nanjing East Road, you will quickly reach the famous Nanjing Road Pedestrian Street, the gaily illuminated shops are an exciting backdrop to the cheerful crowds that come here after dark to enjoy the carefree atmosphere, where it is possible to pick up a bargain or enjoy a tasty morsel to eat.
Metro Line 1 links the three main shopping areas of the city: Nanjing Road, Huanhai Road and Xujiahui. Something that is most convenient for those who like their shopping expeditions! Most of the shops will close at 10 pm but that is when the tea houses and bars really come into their own and the night is still young!
Tea Houses open 24 hours a day. Apart from enjoying a lone taste of tea, you can invite several friends and play cards or just chat. Once you are here, you can experience all this for yourself. Fashionable entertainments are favorites with young people. When night falls, Shanghai bathes in the light of various entertainment venues. Nightclubs, Karaoke, discos, and coffee houses are all popular night time meeting places.
  A cafe in Xintiandi Xintiandi has many visitors. If you are visiting Shanghai for the first time, it is much safer to go Xintiandi for the night life. Xintiandi, the most fashionable area cultivated in the distinctive Shikumen Buildings, the architectural styles of both west and east from the 1920s and 1930s Shanghai around South Huangpi Road and Xingye Road, has become the popular place to go. Every building has a modern interior and has become an international gallery, fashion shop, themed restaurant, coffee house or bar. Bars are where young white collars discuss their work or talk about life; even hard questions on the desk get solved here! Open-air bars are popular here also. Xintiandi offers the most choice and favorable appreciation. The arrival of more and more boutiques, designer shops and luxury goods stores continually adds to the enjoyment of Xintiandi.
ARK Live House is a music restaurant and music bar
Address: No. 15, north block of Xintiandi, No. 181, Taicang Road
Ven Ice is a coffee bar, located at Unit 1, No. 22, north block of Xintiandi, No. 181, Taicang Road
Shanghai's first bars were opened in Hengshan Road, and they remain more popular than those elsewhere. Close to Xujiahui Commercial Circle, Hengshan Road is situated in a convenient situation. Here there are bars in great numbers, side by side and in which you can take tea or coffee. A wide variety of bars ranging from the brash to more intimate and quiet abound to suit your every mood. Thus, Hengshan Road at night can be one of the most bustling places in th city.
Maoming South Road: An upwardly mobile bar street.
This is where the foreign guests like to stay. The old but noted bars like Judystoo are still popular with visitors. Newly-opened Babyface's business is booming. The Colors and Face clubs inside the Ruijin Hotel in the street add their own touch of splendor to this road.
Babyface is a lounge bar and often full of people as it is where young people like to congregate.
Address: No. 180, Maoming South Road Nanjing Road at night Fuxing Park, located at No.2, Haolan Road, is the only well-preserved French park in China, so people also call it "France Garden". Altogether there are three clubs here. They are Park97, Guandi and Cash Box.
Among them, Park97 is where veterans spend their nights through. Three popular food and entertainment grounds, Baci Restaurant of Italian cuisine, Tokio Joe Restaurant with its Japanese cuisine and the California Club from Hong Kong Lan Kwai Fong make up Park97. Compared with that in Xintiandi, nightlife here is not that showy but exudes an everlasting glamour. With elegance, exoticism, top-rank wine and music, Park97 has its special charm. Guandi, the most noted club here, is the first superior club opened in China after Taibei's. Cash Box (Qian Gui) as Shanghai's oldest, most renowned KTV has the largest scale. The branch in Fuxing Park is the best of all in the city.

Shanghai Museum East
 Shanghai Museum East, as a world-class museum of ancient Chinese art, houses a rich collection of ancient relics—from bronzes, sculptures and jade to calligraphy, ceramics and more. Located in Pudong New Area, it is a new branch of the Shanghai Museum fully completed and open to the public in November 2024. It covers 113,200 square meters (27.97 acres) and has eight floors, including six floors above ground and two floors underground. In this grand building, there are a total of 20 exhibition galleries with each relic vividly showcasing the exquisite craftsmanship of ancient Chinese and their avant-garde aesthetic pursuit.
Considering that you may be time-pressed or feel bewildered by the extensive area and massive collections of the Shanghai Museum East upon entering, this guide provides a list of prioritized galleries and cultural relics so as to assist you with an ideal museum tour. Polychrome Glazed Pottery Camel Pensive Bodhisattva  
Must-see Cultural Relics
1. Great Bronze Cauldron (Da Ke Ding) – Bronze Gallery—from Late Western Zhou Dynasty (1046-771 BC)
This is a large bronze ritual tripod cauldron standing 93.1 centimeters (37 inches) high, with a mouth diameter of 75.6 centimeters (30 inches) and a weight of 201.5 kilograms (444 lbs). It features a pair of upright handles on the rim and three robust feet below. The exterior is decorated with beast-mask patterns and wave bands, while the interior wall bears inscriptions that record a noble’s tribute to his grandfather and the royal commissions and rewards he received from the Zhou king. This tripod cauldron represents not only the pinnacle of bronze-casting technology 3,000 years ago, but also an important source of historical material for that period. Great Bronze Cauldron Jade Humanoid Deity   
2. Jade Humanoid Deity – Jade Gallery Bodhisattva in Offering White Marble —from Neolithic Period (Approximately 4200 - 4500 years ago)
It’s a 10.3-centimeter-tall (4-inch-tall) small deity figure carved from greenish-yellow jade, with a flat-topped crown, crossed hands over the chest, and slightly bent knees. This jade figure is considered as an intermediary through whom the prehistoric shaman or tribal leader devoutly communicates with the divine during sacrificial rituals.
3. Bodhisattva in Offering White Marble – Sculpture Gallery—from Tang Dynasty (AD 618-907)
This white marble statue of a bodhisattva stands 70 cm (28 inches) tall and 40 cm (16 inches) wide. It was originally part of a group of devotional figures beneath a main Buddha statue. Carved from solid white marble, the statue delicately captures the soft texture of human skin. The figure has a high piled bun and an ornate crown, with a gentle smile and a serene expression. It is adorned with pearl necklaces, draped scarves, and a long skirt, and kneels barefoot on a lotus base. Although its arms are missing, the statue remains graceful and majestic, representing a masterpiece of high-quality white marble sculpture from the prosperous Tang Dynasty.
4. Sky blue-glazed Plate – Ceramics Gallery  Sky Blue-glazed Plate —from Northern Song Dynasty (AD 960-1127)
With a mouth diameter of 17.1 centimeters (7inches) and luminous sky-blue glaze, this elegant plate is a masterpiece from the most prestigious kiln of the Northern Song Dynasty, which made porcelains exclusively for the imperial court of that era. It’s undeniably a representative artwork, manifesting the incredible craftsmanship of Chinese ceramics in a time when no machines were available for production. 
5. Round Coinage with Square Hole – Numismatics Gallery—from Qin Dynasty (221-207 BC)
Before the Qin Dynasty, currencies varied widely in shape, size and weight across states, causing great inconvenience to trade. After unifying the six rival states, the Qin established a standard round coin with a square hole in the center, which laid the foundation for China’s coinage for over 2,000 years. It also facilitated trade, stabilized the economy and strengthened political rule
Top 5 Unmissable Permanent Galleries
1. Bronze Gallery – 1FBronze Gallery is one of the must-visit galleries at Shanghai Museum East, offering a complete chronological narrative and visual encyclopedia of ancient Chinese bronzes. It presents a nearly uninterrupted collection of bronze artifacts from their emergence, development, flourishing, transformation, and renewal between the 21st century BC and the 3rd century BC. Here you will find a wide variety of bronze objects used as ritual vessels, wine vessels, food vessels, weapons, musical instruments, and other practical tools. Many are decorated with distinctive patterns, including animal masks, dragons, phoenixes, birds, flame motifs, and eye designs. These abundant bronze treasures vividly depict the unique features of ancient Chinese civilization nearly 3,000 years ago.  Bronze Wine Vessel of Western Zhou Ox-shaped Wine Vessel  
2. Sculpture Gallery – 1F Stone Monument of Buddhas The Sculpture Gallery houses a superb collection of ancient Chinese sculptures spanning various dynasties, primarily including gilt-bronze, stone, and wood Buddhist statues, as well as exquisite tomb carvings. It also features other fine sculptural works such as pottery figurines, bone carvings, and ivory carvings. These sculptures artistically illustrate the social beliefs and civilizational exchanges of ancient China across different eras. Here, you can strongly perceive that in contrast to Western classical sculpture, which emphasizes realistic human anatomy and proportion, traditional Chinese sculpture prioritizes overall artistic charm and inner spiritual expression over naturalistic representation.
3. Jade Gallery – 2FChina has long been known as the “land of jade”, with a history of about 10,000 years in jade craftsmanship. This gallery arranges the exhibits along a timeline into six sections, showcasing the development of Chinese jade culture over 8,000 years from prehistoric times to the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911). The roughly 300 pieces of artifacts displayed here, such as jade vessels, jade ornaments, and jade sculptures, are far more than just beautiful objects; they also bear the weight of profound historical narratives. In the early civilizations, the jade served as sacred medium for worship and a symbol of divine power. Later, it became an important part of ritual systems, representing social status and political hierarchy. Influenced by Confucius, jade gradually became a moral symbol associated with virtues. If you appreciate these rarities in a chronological order, you’ll also notice how the craftmanship evolved from simple carvings into delicate openwork and meticulous polishing. Jade in Dragon Shape Jade Cup in Ming Dynasty  
4. Ceramics Gallery & CeraMIX Gallery– 3FJust like the Jade Gallery, the Ceramics Gallery also follows the chronological order to divide the exhibits into seven sections, showing exquisite ceramics from the Neolithic Age to the end of the Qing Dynasty. It presents the complete history of Chinese
